hints: Look closely at the left-hand end of both molecules and notice exactly which functional group changes.
Glucose starts with an aldehyde group, $-CHO$, and sorbitol ends with a primary alcohol group, $-CH_2OH$, so hydrogen is being added.
Adding hydrogen to a carbonyl is reduction, so think about which listed reagent is a classic reducing agent for aldehydes.
walkthrough:
**Spot the functional group change**

Look at carbon 1 on the left. Glucose has $O=CH-$, an aldehyde. Sorbitol has $HO-CH_2-$, a primary alcohol. All the other $OH$ groups are unchanged.

$$\text{-CHO (glucose) } \rightarrow \text{ -CH}_2\text{OH (sorbitol)}$$

**Classify as reduction or oxidation**

Converting $C=O$ to $CH_2O$ means gaining hydrogen. That is reduction of the aldehyde. So we need a reducing agent, not an oxidising agent.

$$\text{R-CHO + 2[H] } \rightarrow \text{ R-CH}_2\text{OH}$$

**Choose the correct reagent**

Sodium borohydride, $NaBH_4$, is the standard mild reducing agent that reduces aldehydes and ketones to alcohols. The other reagents are oxidisers or bases, so they cannot do this reduction.

options.A: Acidified potassium dichromate(VI) is a strong oxidising agent. It would oxidise the aldehyde in glucose further, not reduce it to an alcohol, so it gives the opposite type of reaction.
options.B: Sodium borohydride provides hydride, $H^-$, and reduces aldehydes to primary alcohols. Here it cleanly reduces the $-CHO$ of glucose to $-CH_2OH$ to give sorbitol, leaving the other alcohol groups untouched.
options.C: Sodium hydroxide is a base, not a reducing agent. It has no source of hydrogen to reduce $C=O$ and would not convert an aldehyde to a primary alcohol.
options.D: Tollens reagent is a mild oxidising agent used to test for aldehydes. It oxidises an aldehyde to a carboxylate ion, so glucose would be oxidised, not reduced to sorbitol.
